newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: EU pledges open telecoms market in trade pact bid.
newsitem.headline: EU pledges open telecoms market in trade pact bid.

text.p: The European Union Tuesday offered a wide-ranging opening of its telecommunications market in a concerted bid with the United States to clinch a World Trade Organisation pact by next February.

The EU offer, presented at high-level negotiations on a global deal, was expected to be followed by new proposals from Washington, which balked at joining a WTO deal in April because it felt other nations were holding back.

The move followed talks between the two top trade powers in Chicago over the weekend, and senior EU negotiator Karl-Fredrik Falkenberg said the EU was acting "in a coordinated way" with the United States.

U.S. Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang told envoys from the 125 WTO member nations Monday that Washington would improve its earlier offer by, among other innovations, opening local exchange markets to foreign trade and investment.

Falkenberg told a news conference that he hoped countries at the two-year-old WTO's first ministerial meeting in Singapore next month would agree on some "robust language" of commitment to the Feb. 15 deadline.
A WTO pact would make signatory powers bound by rules reinforced through a disputes settlement procedure that would effectively force countries found in violation of the accord to shape up.

Under the new EU package Spain, whose former Socialist government had been reluctant to open up its domestic telecommunications market to foreign competition before 2003, will now liberalise starting in January 1998.

The earlier hardline stand from the Spanish, whose telecommunications sector is regarded as potentially one of Europe's most lucrative, had been cited by U.S. officials as a major defect in the EU offer in previous WTO talks.
"We think this is now completing the opening for the European Community for major markets," Falkenberg said.
Ireland would not fully liberalise until the year 2000, and Greece and Portugal until 2003, but these were "marginal" markets, he said.

After 18 months of negotiations, some 50 countries failed in April to meet a deadline to shape a pact in the rapidly growing sector after U.S. officials said a "critical mass" of offers had not been reached.

The EU -- together with the world's other two top trade powers, Canada and Japan -- had been ready to make a deal on the basis of packages put up at that time, including by the emerging economies from whom the United States wanted more.

Under the new EU offer, previous foreign investment restrictions in Spain and Belgium and indirect restrictions in the telecommunications sector in France were withdrawn, and all limits on foreign satellite services were dropped.
Liberalisation of mobile telephone services in all 15 EU states was brought forward to 1998, with what Falkenberg said were "minor regulatory provisions" for Ireland and Portugal.

But Falkenberg said the offer was conditional on getting significant improvements from other WTO members in the talks. The EU wanted better terms from Canada and Japan as well as from developing countries like Singapore, Korea and Brazil, he said.

He told reporters that Brussels wanted the United States to end restrictions on submarine cable landings and commit itself to giving equal -- or MFN most-favoured-nation -- treatment to all trade partners in all telecommunications services.

The EU wanted withdrawal of Canadian foreign investment restrictions and sought MFN commitments also from Japan. It wanted elimination of foreign investment restrictions in Singapore, South Korea and Mexico and liberalisation of all telecommunications services in Brazil by 1998.
